title: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
description: We look at new PPNs 024 and 025 on insourcing strategy and national security.

content_blocks.text: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025

content_blocks.text: The Government has issued two new Procurement Policy Notes which, read together, signal a more deliberate and strategic use of public procurement. PPN 025 focuses on protecting national security through procurement decisions, while PPN 024 introduces a formal Public Interest Test and a clearer expectation that authorities consider insourcing alongside outsourcing.
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025

content_blocks.text: PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement

content_blocks.text: PPN 025 is driven by the Government’s National Security Strategy 2025, which highlights a major cultural shift in how public procurement should be used to protect national security. The PPN makes clear that national security now extends beyond defence and includes supporting critical sectors and securing supply chains so they can be relied upon in times of crisis. The policy identifies four sectors as particularly important: shipbuilding, steel, artificial intelligence and energy infrastructure.
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement

content_blocks.text: The PPN sets out three core actions for contracting authorities:
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement

content_blocks.text: Identify the procurements in their pipeline that are relevant to the sectors listed above and assess their national security implications, including supply chain vulnerabilities and dependency risks.
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement

content_blocks.text: Engage early with the relevant Sector Lead, who will provide coordination, market insight and support in developing the commercial approach.
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement

content_blocks.text: Consider whether to deploy the national security exemption in the Procurement Act 2023, where appropriate and justified. The accompanying guidance makes clear that use of the exemption must be justified on a case-by-case basis and supported by an evidence-based rationale, with decisions recorded and aligned with the UK’s trade obligations. It also emphasises that procurement should be used as a tool for market shaping, including managing supply risk and strengthening long-term resilience.
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement

content_blocks.text: In practical terms, PPN 025 will require contracting authorities to incorporate national security considerations into routine procurement planning and to engage more closely with central government. For suppliers, particularly in the identified sectors, there is likely to be increased focus on supply chain security, resilience and alignment with wider government priorities.
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement

content_blocks.text: PPN 024: The Public Interest Test and insourcing strategy
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement
PPN 024: The Public Interest Test and insourcing strategy

content_blocks.text: PPN 024 complements this shift by focusing on how authorities decide whether to outsource services at all. It introduces a structured Public Interest Test, designed to ensure that decisions about outsourcing or insourcing are made on a broader and more consistent basis.
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement
PPN 024: The Public Interest Test and insourcing strategy

content_blocks.text: The core premise is that authorities should not assume that outsourcing is the default model. Instead, they are expected to assess delivery options in the round, taking into account factors such as value for money over the long term, service quality, resilience, and the strategic importance of the service. The emphasis is on determining what best serves the public interest, rather than what is cheapest or most convenient in the short term.
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement
PPN 024: The Public Interest Test and insourcing strategy

content_blocks.text: Alongside this, the PPN requires authorities to take a more proactive approach to insourcing strategy. This includes considering whether services could be delivered in-house and, where appropriate, building the capability to do so. The intention is to support greater control over critical or sensitive services and to ensure continuity and resilience of delivery.
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement
PPN 024: The Public Interest Test and insourcing strategy

content_blocks.text: A key practical requirement is that the Public Interest Test must be properly evidenced and documented before a procurement is launched. This may lead to fewer opportunities going to market where authorities conclude that in-house delivery better meets their objectives.
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement
PPN 024: The Public Interest Test and insourcing strategy

content_blocks.text: For suppliers, the impact is likely to be most visible at renewal stage, where authorities may revisit delivery models rather than automatically re-procuring existing contracts. Suppliers will therefore need to engage earlier and demonstrate how their offering supports not just cost efficiency, but also wider outcomes such as resilience and service quality.
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement
PPN 024: The Public Interest Test and insourcing strategy

content_blocks.text: A more strategic procurement landscape
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement
A more strategic procurement landscape

content_blocks.text: Both PPN 024 and PPN 025 point towards a more interventionist and strategic approach to public procurement. Authorities are expected to think beyond immediate delivery needs and consider how their decisions affect national resilience, market capability and long-term public value.
heading_path: Procurement Policy Notes: PPN 024 and PPN 025
PPN 025: Protecting the UK’s national security through procurement
A more strategic procurement landscape

content_blocks.text: Procurement processes are likely to become more complex and more closely aligned with government policy objectives. Early engagement, robust analysis and clear documentation will be essential to navigate this evolving landscape. At the same time, suppliers will need to adapt by demonstrating not just competitiveness on price, but also their contribution to broader strategic goals.
